body_markdown:
Learn how to store fruits and vegetables properly with five simple expert tips that can help reduce spoilage, extend freshness and cut household food waste.


Fresh fruits and vegetables can quickly lose their quality when they are stored in the wrong conditions. Wilted herbs, mouldy berries, soft carrots and spoiled greens are common sights in household fridges, but many of these problems can be prevented with a few simple storage changes.


The way produce is handled after shopping can make a significant difference to how long it remains fresh. Moisture, temperature, airflow and the natural ripening process all influence how quickly fruit and vegetables deteriorate.


Food safety experts and dietitians recommend several practical changes, from delaying washing until you are ready to eat produce to keeping certain foods away from one another.


Here are five expert-backed ways to keep your fruits and vegetables fresher for longer.


## 1. Do not wash produce until you are ready to eat it


One of the easiest ways to extend the shelf life of fresh produce is to avoid washing it immediately after bringing it home.


Although washing fruits and vegetables may seem like a sensible preparation step, leftover water can create a damp environment where bacteria, yeast and mould can multiply more easily.


Instead, store most produce dry and wash it shortly before eating or cooking.


This is particularly useful for delicate foods such as berries and leafy greens. If you have already washed these foods, make sure they are thoroughly dried before storing them.


Paper towels can also help absorb excess moisture in containers holding berries or salad leaves. Replacing a damp towel when necessary can help prevent moisture from accumulating.


Cutting produce before storage can also shorten its usable life. Once a fruit or vegetable is cut, its internal surfaces are exposed to air and moisture, which can accelerate deterioration.


For the longest possible shelf life, keep fruits and vegetables whole until you need them.


## 2. Use your fridge wisely and avoid overcrowding


Temperature plays a major role in food freshness. Many fruits and vegetables last longer when kept chilled, because lower temperatures can slow the growth of microorganisms responsible for spoilage.


However, simply putting everything in the refrigerator is not always the best solution.


An overcrowded fridge can restrict airflow and make it more difficult for cold air to circulate evenly. Leaving enough space between items can help maintain more consistent temperatures.


Different types of produce also have different storage requirements.


Fresh herbs, for example, can often benefit from being treated similarly to flowers. Trim the stems and place the herbs in a container with a small amount of water. Some hardier herbs can instead be wrapped in a slightly damp towel before being refrigerated.


Carrots can also benefit from moisture. Storing them properly can help them retain their crisp texture. If carrots or beets have leafy tops attached, removing the tops before storage may help the roots stay fresh for longer because the leaves draw moisture from them.


The key is to avoid using one storage method for every type of produce. Understanding the needs of individual foods can make a noticeable difference.


## 3. Keep certain foods away from each other


Where you store produce can affect both its quality and its shelf life.


Tomatoes are a good example. While refrigeration can slow spoilage, keeping whole tomatoes at room temperature can help preserve their flavour and texture.


Garlic also has different requirements depending on its condition. Whole garlic generally does best in a cool, dry and well-ventilated location. Once garlic has been peeled or cut, it should be refrigerated.


Potatoes and onions should also be stored separately. Both prefer a cool, dark and well-ventilated environment, but keeping them together can encourage faster deterioration.


Another important consideration is ethylene gas.


Some fruits naturally release ethylene as they ripen. This plant hormone can accelerate ripening in nearby produce. As a result, placing very ripe bananas alongside other fruit may cause neighbouring produce to ripen more quickly.


Separating foods according to their ripening behaviour can therefore help extend their useful life.


## 4. Learn the difference between ageing and spoilage


Not every fruit or vegetable that looks less than perfect needs to go into the bin.


Some changes in appearance or texture are signs that produce has lost quality rather than evidence that it has become unsafe.


For example, a carrot that has become slightly limp may still be suitable for cooking. Celery that has lost some of its crunch can often be used in soups, stews or cooked dishes.


Wilted leafy vegetables may also be usable depending on their condition.


Understanding the difference between food quality and food safety can help households reduce unnecessary waste.


However, there are signs that should not be ignored. Visible mould, slimy surfaces, leaking liquid and strong unpleasant odours can indicate that produce has deteriorated significantly.


When in doubt, it is important to prioritise food safety rather than attempting to rescue food that shows clear signs of spoilage.


## 5. Plan meals and freeze produce before it spoils


Good storage habits work best when combined with sensible shopping and meal planning.


Buying more fruit and vegetables than your household can realistically use often leads to unnecessary waste. Before shopping, check what you already have and consider which foods need to be eaten first.


A simple "first in, first out" approach can help. Place older produce where it is easy to see and keep newer purchases behind it.


Freezing is another useful option when fresh produce is approaching the end of its best quality. Berries, bananas and some vegetables can be frozen and later used in smoothies, baking, sauces and cooked meals.


You can also adapt recipes around what needs to be eaten soonest. Soft vegetables can become soups, stews or roasted side dishes, while ripe fruit can be used in smoothies or desserts.


Reducing food waste is not only about saving money. Food that is thrown away represents wasted land, water, energy, transport and labour used throughout the food supply chain.


When discarded food ends up in landfill, its decomposition can also contribute to methane emissions. That means simple household habits, repeated across millions of homes, can have a wider environmental impact.


## Small storage changes can make a big difference


Keeping fruits and vegetables fresh for longer does not require complicated equipment or expensive storage systems.


Start with a few basic habits: keep produce dry until you need it, avoid unnecessary cutting, maintain good airflow in the fridge, separate foods that can speed up each other's ripening and learn to recognise genuine signs of spoilage.


It is also worth remembering that imperfect-looking produce is not automatically waste. A slightly soft carrot or wilted vegetable may still have plenty of uses.


By storing food carefully, shopping with a plan and using produce before it deteriorates, households can save money while throwing away less food.


The most effective approach is consistency. Small changes to how you store everyday groceries can add up over time, helping your fruit and vegetables stay fresher and making your kitchen more efficient.


**Source:** *The Independent* , August 22, 2026.


**Disclaimer:** This article is for general informational purposes only and is not a substitute for official food safety guidance. Storage recommendations can vary depending on the type and condition of produce. If food shows clear signs of spoilage, such as visible mould, slime, leaking liquid or a strong unpleasant smell, follow appropriate food safety guidance and discard it when necessary.
